questions.q: Why are excursions said to form the *first and lasting impression* of a destination?
options: Because they are always the cheapest tourist service
Because tourists often have limited time, so one excursion can define their whole perception of a country or city
Because excursions are compulsory for all tourists
questions.explain: Topic 1: tourists spend limited time in one place, so a good or bad excursion strongly shapes the destination's image and word-of-mouth.

questions.q: Which of the following are functions of excursions named in the lecture on their importance?
options: Spreading tourist flows beyond city centres
questions.explain: Topic 1: excursions educate, spread tourism spatially and brand the destination; they do not replace transport.

questions.q: According to the lecture, promoting excursions to rural and ecological destinations beyond Almaty and Astana can stimulate regional development in Kazakhstan.
questions.explain: Topic 1 (and 15): this is the lecture's Kazakhstan example of using excursions to reduce spatial tourism inequality.

questions.q: Who organised the first package tours in Britain in the 1840s, including transport, meals and guided interpretation?
questions.explain: Topic 2: Thomas Cook's model set a template for future excursion services during the Industrial Revolution.

options: A medieval pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela
Renaissance-era educational travel of wealthy European aristocrats, mainly to Italy and France
A Soviet state system of excursion planning
A 19th-century German school walk to factories
questions.explain: Topic 2: the Grand Tour included visits to galleries, ruins and universities guided by tutors; it was a precursor of cultural excursions.

questions.q: Which statement best describes excursion studies in the Soviet Union?
options: Market-oriented and based on private tour companies
Highly formalised and integrated into state ideological and cultural policy, with systematic classification and textbooks
questions.explain: Topic 2: Soviet excursion studies became a centralised applied discipline and a form of mass education.

questions.q: What is described as the **core** of excursion service?
options: Physical movement of the group between sites
The guide's knowledge, storytelling ability and communicative skill
questions.explain: Topic 3: the essence of an excursion is the narrative; an unprofessional guide can spoil even a valuable attraction.

questions.q: In Kazakhstan, certified guides must complete specialised training and show knowledge of history, culture and foreign languages before leading groups.
questions.explain: Topic 3: this is the lecture's example of the legal and professional framework of excursion service.

questions.q: A street is suddenly closed during a city tour and the guide changes the route on the spot. Which peculiarity of excursion service does this illustrate?
options: Its time-limited and mobile nature, requiring real-time decisions
questions.explain: Topic 3: excursions move between sites in limited time, so the guide needs situational awareness and adaptability.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the phases in the structure of an excursion?
questions.explain: Topic 4: the structured phases are preparation, introduction, main body and conclusion.

questions.q: According to the classification by duration, a *short* excursion lasts:
questions.explain: Topic 4: duration types are short (up to 2 hours), half-day, full-day and multi-day.

questions.q: Which of these are types of excursions **by purpose**?
questions.explain: Topic 4: by purpose excursions are educational, recreational, aesthetic, religious/pilgrimage and commemorative; 'walking' is a form of movement.

questions.q: Which definition of **excursion objects** matches the lecture?
options: Material and immaterial components of a destination with cultural, historical, natural, aesthetic, scientific or symbolic significance, selected for interpretation
Any place where tourists can buy souvenirs
Only objects on the UNESCO list
questions.explain: Topic 5: excursion objects can be tangible or intangible and are chosen for interpretation and presentation to visitors.

questions.q: The ALZHIR complex near Astana is an example of which type of excursion object?
questions.explain: Topic 5: ALZHIR commemorates women imprisoned during Stalin's repressions and needs empathetic, careful interpretation.

questions.q: Which Kazakhstan site does the lecture give as an example of an **industrial and technological** excursion object?
questions.explain: Topic 5: Baikonur is an active technological site, which requires coordination with the host and strict safety rules.

questions.q: In the methodology of excursion preparation, what is the **excursion plan**?
options: The interpretive text spoken at each stop
A document with the structure, timing, logistics, emergency contacts, permissions and backup scenarios of the tour
A list of legends about the city
questions.explain: Topic 6: the plan is the organisational document; the script (commentary) is the text delivered at each stop.

questions.q: According to the methodology, evaluation and feedback are optional and are not part of excursion preparation.
questions.explain: Topic 6: evaluation and feedback (surveys, discussions, observation) are a key, though often overlooked, stage used to improve future excursions.

questions.q: Which of the following does the lecture treat as components of the **quality** of excursion service?
options: Ethical standards such as fair wages for guides and transparent pricing
Presenting legends as facts to make the tour more exciting
questions.explain: Topic 7: content accuracy, logistics and ethics are all quality components; legends presented as facts reduce quality.
